paras: The whitecapping of Bill Pierce was the night beating of William (Bill) Pierce, a Black resident of Lake Park, Georgia, by a party of white men on August 7, 1905, after he refused an order to leave the community. Pierce swore out warrants against five men described as prominent citizens, among them a justice of the peace and a merchant whose whiskey case he was to testify in, and they were placed under bond for superior court.

Pierce was said to be a witness against R. W. Wheeler, a Lake Park merchant accused of selling whiskey without a license. Several days before the attack he was ordered to leave the community at once, the object being, according to the Associated Press, "to get rid of his testimony in a whiskey selling case." He consulted other citizens, who advised him not to leave.

On Monday night a party of men went to his house, took him out and beat him. In the Associated Press account a buggy drove up during the attack and frightened the men away, leaving Pierce "half dead." A Valdosta report of the next day said instead that citizens who came to his rescue while he was being flogged were driven off by the attackers, who drew pistols, and that he was rescued later.

On August 9 Pierce swore out warrants at Valdosta, according to the dispatches "under the advice of white citizens," charging the men with assault with intent to murder. Those named were Justice of the Peace W. T. Corbett, Wheeler, D. W. Damer, Henry Connell and Paul Coler, with the spellings varying from paper to paper. Deputy Sheriff Crosby went to Lake Park to serve the warrants, and the August 10 report gave the charge as rioting and said each man was placed under a $200 bond to appear at the next term of the superior court. No report of a trial or its outcome was found.

The Associated Press report ran on August 10 and 11 in the Newport News Daily Press under the headline "Tried to Drive the Negro Away," in the Raleigh News & Observer as "For Whitecapping a Negro," and in shortened form in the Richmond Times Dispatch. The Birmingham Age-Herald's own Valdosta dispatch led with "White Men Charged With Whitecapping" and, like the wire, stressed that the warrants had white backing. The Gainesville Daily Sun printed the follow-up on the arrests and bonds on August 11.

The only Black-press report found, a front-page brief in the Savannah Tribune on August 12, used the same Valdosta follow-up almost word for word under the headline "Prominent Men Arrested for Alleged Beating of a Colored Witness." Where the Gainesville text gave the charge as rioting, the Tribune gave it as whitecapping, and like the white papers it added no comment.

The accounts differ on how the beating ended: the August 9 wire credited a passing buggy, while the August 10 dispatch described armed whitecappers driving off rescuers. The charge also appears as assault with intent to murder, rioting or whitecapping, depending on the report.

reader.title: Whitecapping of Bill Pierce
bases: A party of men ordered Pierce to leave the community and, when he stayed, took him from his house at night and beat him, an act every report headlined or described as 'whitecapping' (A1, A2, A4, A6).

The Associated Press report of Aug. 9 (A1, A5), a separately worded Valdosta dispatch the same day (A2) and a Valdosta follow-up of Aug. 10 (A4, followed by A6) agree on the order to leave, the night beating and the warrants against named Lake Park men, though all originate in Valdosta and differ on details.

accounts.label: Associated Press, Valdosta, Aug. 9
accounts.gist: A party of men took Pierce from his house Monday night and beat him until a buggy drove up and frightened them away, leaving him half dead; he swore out warrants for assault with intent to murder.

accounts.label: Valdosta dispatch, Aug. 9
accounts.gist: Same sequence in separate wording, with four men named and the beating called a 'drubbing'.

accounts.label: Valdosta dispatch, Aug. 10
accounts.gist: Warrants served on five prominent citizens; citizens who came to the rescue during the flogging were driven off by the whitecappers' pistols, and Pierce was later rescued; the men were bonded for superior court.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'Tried to Drive the Negro Away' and 'For Whitecapping a Negro' carried the wire text, put the motive as getting rid of his testimony, and stressed that white citizens backed the warrants.
The Birmingham Age-Herald headlined 'White Men Charged With Whitecapping' and noted the warrants were sworn 'under the advice of white citizens'.
The Savannah Tribune ran the Valdosta follow-up as a front-page brief headlined 'Prominent Men Arrested for Alleged Beating of a Colored Witness', without comment.

conflicts.note: The Aug. 10 follow-up is later but neither version is attributed to a named witness.
The Savannah Tribune text otherwise follows the same Aug. 10 dispatch as the Gainesville Sun, so its 'whitecapping' may be an editorial substitution.
